text: Introduction to Large Language Models Lecture 1, Part 2: A lifecycle of LLM Xingyi Yang Hong Kong Polytechnic University A Simple Request Starts the Journey Me Plan a PolyU-to-Victoria-Peak trip for tomorrow. Check the weather first. ChatGPT Let me check tomorrow’s weather before suggesting the route. The reply takes seconds. What had to happen before? One Answer Runs on Two Clocks ⏱️ What the user sees A few seconds One request → one answer ≠ 🏗️ What makes it possible Months of preparation A model built earlier + a system working now One minute on stage, years behind the scenes. The Model Learned Before You Asked The weather is ___ sunny · rainy · cold Across a very large collection of text, the model repeatedly

asks: What token is likely to come next? Repeated prediction builds broad language and knowledge patterns. Then It Learned to Be Helpful Human Request + Good Response → Helpful Assistant Demonstrations Preferences Show what a good response Show which response is more should look like. useful, clear, and safe. Later, we will call these ideas SFT and preference-based reinforcement learning. Press Send: The System Builds Context For this trip request, the application gathers only what the model can use now. Instructio Trip + History + + Tool info → Context ns request Prepared by the application Changes with this request System instructions Trip request and conversation history Tool definitions and permissions Retrieved evidence and tool results Context is the model’s working desk for this request.

Text Becomes Tokens the Model Can Process Text → Tokens → Token IDs The Model Generates One Token at a Time Current context ↓ Transformer ↓ Next-token probabilities ↓ Select one token and repeat Each new token becomes part of the context for the next prediction. Fresh Weather Requires a Tool Missing Request Add result Complete → → → weather weather data to context the plan ChatGPT Morning: PolyU → Central · Afternoon: Victoria Peak Weather-aware tip: move the Peak visit earlier if rain is expected later. The application runs the tool; the model decides how to use its result. The Answer Returns—and Leaves Evidence Response delivered User signals Task signals System signals Rating, correction, retry, or a Did the route, answer, or tool Latency,

tool errors, unsafe or changed request call succeed? low-quality output A response ends one request—but it can become evidence for the next model version. The Full Loop: Build, Execute, Improve Offline — Build Prepare data → Pre-train → Post-train → Evaluate & release Online — Execute Build context → Generate → Use tools or agents → Return a response Feedback — Improve Observe outcomes → Curate data → Improve the next model or system version Offline builds. Online executes. Feedback improves. Contents A. An LLM Learns From a Very Large Library Web + Books + Code + Examples Pages and articles Long-form writing Programs and docs Carefully selected tasks The model does not read like a person—it learns recurring patterns across tokens. Data Is Not Automatically Usable ⚖️ 🤐 Rights Privacy 🛡️ ✅ Safety Quality “Available” does not mean appropriate for training. Vet every source before it teaches the model. Clean the Library Before Training Raw Filter Remove Training → → → Deduplicate → corpus quality spam corpus Garbage in, garbage out—repeated or poor text can teach the wrong lesson many times. The Data Mixture Is the Model's Diet More code can improve programming skills. Language More languages can improve multilingual coverage. Better sources can improve reliability.

A model trained only on cookbooks may Domains Quality write great recipes—but struggle with Python. Tokenization Creates a Discrete Sequence Text → Tokens → Token IDs Contents A. Pre-training Is Still Machine Learning Fit a model to text by minimizing prediction loss. 1. Objective 2. Training 3. Model Predict the next token Backprop + optimizer Transformer Distributed training runs the same optimization across many GPUs.

Objective: Predict the Next Token Given the context… The cat sat on the _____ mat 46% floor 24% sofa 12% … Actual next token: mat Objective: give the actual token high probability by minimizing cross-entropy loss. Objective: Self-Supervision from Raw Text No human labels The text provides both context and target. RAW TEXT CREATES A TRAINING PAIR The cat sat on the → mat context target Repeat at every token The corpus bootstraps its own supervision. Raw corpus → automatic targets → scalable pre-training Step 1: Make a Prediction FORWARD PASS Context x LLM Prediction from raw text parameters θ P(next token) Prediction: context x → next-token probabilities.

Step 2: Compute Loss and Gradients FORWARD PASS Context x LLM Prediction Loss from raw text parameters θ P(next token) compare with target y BACKPROPAGATION Compute gradients dL/dθ via the chain rule Self-supervised target: y comes from the same text; backprop gives dL/dθ. Step 3: Optimize the Parameters FORWARD PASS Context x LLM Prediction Loss from raw text parameters θ P(next token) compare with target y BACKPROPAGATION Optimizer updates θ Compute gradients θ ← θ − η · dL/dθ dL/dθ via the chain rule Optimization: use dL/dθ to update θ, then repeat. Model: A Transformer Connects the Context Tokens need context. In “river bank”, river clarifies bank. Self-attention connects each position with relevant earlier tokens. Stacked layers produce next-token probabilities.

Modern LLMs typically use a decoder-only variant. Diagram: original Transformer architecture from Vaswani et al. (2017). Distributed Training Makes Scale Possible Split Divide data or the model across GPUs. Synchronize Exchange gradients during training. Scale Train larger models in practical time. Same objective, distributed computation. The Result Is a Base Model Massive text corpus Base model Language, code, and many → Generates plausible domains continuations from context It learns broad patterns—but prediction is not the same as helpfulness. A Base Model Is Not an Assistant Yet What it can do What it cannot reliably do Continue text fluently Follow user intent Imitate learned patterns Stay factual Generate code or prose Behave safely Post-training is needed to shape the predictor into a useful assistant. Offline: How an LLM Is Built ▶ Prepare Data & Model ▶ Pre-train the Base Model ▶ Post-train the Assistant ▶ Optimize & Release Core question: How do demonstrations and preferences turn a predictor into an assistant? Post-training Teaches Desired Behavior A pre-trained model predicts plausible text—it is not yet a reliable assistant. Pre-training builds capability; post-training shapes default behavior. Example: Show How to Follow a Request Instruction Good response “Summarize in one sentence: → “The launch is now scheduled for Friday.” The launch moved from Monday to Friday.” One demonstration = instruction + desired response Supervised Fine-tuning from Demonstrations Training examples Collect instruction–response pairs. Fine-tune Update the pre-trained model on those examples. Adapt Examples can target domains such as medicine, law, or finance.

Collect examples of the behavior you want. Reinforcement Learning Uses Preferences Response A Response B Clear and follows the Vague or incomplete request A is preferred over B Preference → Reward → Optimize Choose which response is better. RL makes preferred responses more likely. Post-training Can Shape Many Behaviors 🧩 Problem solving Worked examples + correctness feedback 🛡️ Safety When to answer, refuse, or redirect 🔧 Tool use When and how to call a tool Show good behavior. Reinforce better choices. The Result Is a Post-trained Assistant Base model Post-trained model Predicts a plausible continuation → Follows instructions like an assistant Broad knowledge, weak behavioral control More useful and safer by default Better behavior still does not guarantee correctness. DSAI4207 Introduction to Large Language Models Lecture 2: Probabilistic Language Modeling Xingyi Yang Hong Kong Polytechnic University A Simple Example “The water of Walden Pond is beautifully …” clear green refrigerator highly likely plausible highly unlikely Given the same context, some continuations are more likely than others. What Does a Language Model Do? A language model assigns probabilities to possible continuations. Context in → probabilities over what may come next. You Already Use Language Models Every Day You Already Use Language Models Every Day Chat, search, writing, and code completion all repeatedly ask the same question: what comes next? One Blank, Many Abilities A simple next-token prediction can require surprisingly rich knowledge.

World “PolyU is located in …” Hong Kong Knowledge Coreference “Mei checked traffic over … shoulder.” her “Iroh went into the kitchen to make tea. Commonsense Zuko followed him into the …” kitchen Pattern 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … 21 Reasoning Why Does Next-Token Prediction Matter? Free Text supplies its own prediction targets at massive Supervision scale. Predict Good prediction can require language, facts, context, Requires and reasoning. Understand Unified Many tasks can be expressed as: given a context, Paradigm predict what comes next. A deceptively simple prediction task can provide a remarkably powerful learning signal. Language Modeling At position t, the context is everything we have observed so far: x<t = (x1 , … , xt−1 ).

​ ​ ​ A language model assigns a probability to every possible next token: pθ (v ∣ x<t ), ​ ​ v ∈ V. ∑ pθ (v ∣ x<t ) = 1. ​ ​ ​ v∈V Context in → probability distribution out. How Do We Learn to Predict the Next Token? ① Context → ② Predict → ③ Observe → ④ Learn I like pθ(· | I like) tea ↑ pθ(tea | I like) Training goal: assign higher probability to the continuations observed in real text. From One Token to a Sequence If every position has a next-token probability, can we assign a probability to an entire sequence? T pθ (x1:T ) = ∏ pθ (xt ∣ x<t ).

​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ t=1 This → is → fun Preview: we will derive this factorization from the probability chain rule in Chapter 1. A sequence score is built from a chain of local next-token predictions. Language Modeling as Optimization Training asks us to choose parameters that give observed continuations high probability. T arg max ∑ ∑ log pθ (xt ∣ x<t ) ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ θ x1:T ∈D t=1 ​ 𝒟 = training corpus · x1:T = one sequence · x<t = context · xt = observed next token · θ = parameters Choose θ so that real next tokens receive high probability.

Why Toss a Coin? Which team starts? Which end does each team defend? We know what can happen, but not which outcome will occur. Probability describes this uncertainty. Random Experiment, Outcome, and Sample Space Toss one fair coin once. Random experiment An action whose result is uncertain. Outcome One possible result: Heads H or Tails T.

Sample space The set of all possible outcomes. Ω = {H, T} Probability Foundations 17 / 101 Random Variable and Observed Value Let X denote the result of the coin toss. X ∈ {H, T }. Before the toss: X After observing Heads: The result is uncertain. x=H X may take the value H or T. One value has been observed. Lowercase x denotes this observed value. A random variable represents an uncertain value; an observation tells us which value actually occurred. Probability Foundations 18 / 101 A Probability Distribution Assigns the Chances Assign a probability to each value P(X = H) = 0.5 P(X = T) = 0.5 Add all possible values P(X = H) + P(X = T) = 1 General rule P(X

= x) ≥ 0 Σx P(X = x) = 1 A probability distribution assigns non-negative probability to every possible value, and the probabilities sum to one. Probability Foundations 19 / 101 What If We Toss the Coin Twice? Toss a fair coin twice, with the two tosses independent. Event A: at least one Head HH ✓ HT ✓ TH ✓ TT ✗ A = {HH, HT, TH} P(A) = ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = ¾ Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT} Each outcome has probability 1/4. An event is a set of outcomes. Its probability is the total probability of the matching outcomes. Probability Foundations 20 / 101 Expectation: What Is the Average?

To compute a numerical average, encode Heads as 1 and Tails as 0. Z={ 1, X = H, 0, X = T. ​ ​ H T H H T T H T 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 E[Z] = 0.5(1) + 0.5(0) = 0.5. Expectation is the probability-weighted average value. Probability Foundations 21 / 101 Variance: How Much Does It Vary? Expectation describes the center. Variance describes how much the values spread around it. 2 Var(Z) = E [(Z − E[Z]) ] . Var(Z) = 0.5(1 − 0.5)2 + 0.5(0 − 0.5)2 = 0.25. ​ ​ Expectation describes the center; variance describes the spread around it. Probability Foundations 22 / 101 From Coins to Tokens The probability rules stay the same.

Only the possible values change. Coin toss Language model Variable: X Values: H, T Variable: Xt Values: tokens in 𝒱 H 0.50 tea 0.50 T 0.50 coffee 0.30 water 0.15 P(H) + P(T) = 1 others 0.05 Σv∈𝒱 pθ(v | x<t) = 1 The same probability rules apply. A language model assigns the mass to tokens. Probability Foundations 23 / 101 A Language Model Is Like a Huge Biased Die Rolling the die = sampling the next token. Many sides One side for each token in the vocabulary. Weighted Some tokens are more likely than others. Context changes it Different context, different probabilities. A language model is a weighted die whose probabilities change with the context.

Probability Foundations 24 / 101 A Tiny Language World The coin gave us the probability vocabulary. Now let us apply the same ideas to language. <s> I like tea <e> <s> I like coffee <e> <s> You like tea <e> S = Subject D = Drink I or You tea or coffee Sample one sentence uniformly. Now the uncertain outcomes are words and language sequences. Probability Foundations 25 / 101 Joint Distribution: What Happens Together? For one sampled sentence, look at the subject S and drink D together. P(S, D) D = tea D = coffee S=I 1/3 1/3 S = You 1/3 0 1/3 0 S = I and D = tea occur together. S = You and D = coffee never occur.

A joint distribution assigns probability to combinations of variables. Probability Foundations 26 / 101 Marginal Distribution: Ignore One Variable What if we care about the subject but not the drink? P(S, D) tea coffee row sum S=I 1/3 1/3 2/3 S = You 1/3 0 1/3 column sum 2/3 1/3 1 P (S = s) = ∑ P (S = s, D = d) ​ d To marginalize a variable, sum over all of its possible values. Select S = I 1/3 tea 1/3 coffee total = 2/3 divide by 2/3 P(D | S = I) 1/2 tea 1/2 coffee sum = 1 P (S

= s, D = d) P (D = d ∣ S = s) = P (S = s) ​ Conditioning fixes one context and renormalizes the remaining possibilities. P (S = s, D = d) = P (S = s) P (D = d ∣ S = s) subject drink given subject joint × = P(S=I)=2/3 P(D=tea|S=I)=1/2 P(I,tea)=1/3 Joint = Marginal × Conditional. Probability Foundations 29 / 101 Chain Rule of Probability Apply the product rule repeatedly through a sequence.

T p(x1:T ) = ∏ p(xt ∣ x<t ) ​ ​ ​ ​ t=1 choose choose choose I → like → tea 2/3 1 1/2 2 1 1 p(I like tea) = × 1 × = 3 2 3 ​ ​ ​ A sequence probability is a product of local conditional probabilities. No independence assumption is required. Probability Foundations 30 / 101 The Chain Rule Becomes a Language Model A language model puts parameters into each conditional distribution. Chain rule term Learned model p(xt | x<t) → pθ(xt | x<t) T pθ (x1:T ) = ∏ pθ (xt ∣ x<t ) ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ t=1 The modeling problem is now clear: learn the next-token distribution for every context.

P(coffee | I) P(I | coffee) Among sentences with subject I, how Among sentences with coffee, how many use coffee? many have subject I? 1/2 1 P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different conditional distributions. P (D = coffee ∣ S = I) P (S = I) P (S = I ∣ D = coffee) = P (D = coffee) ​ conditional marginal evidence × ÷ = 1 1/2 2/3 1/3 Useful probability tool, but autoregressive language models mainly rely on the chain rule.

If knowing the subject changes the drink distribution, the variables are dependent. information P(tea) what happened? subject unknown 2/3 baseline subject = I 1/2 changed subject = You 1 changed S⊥ D ⟺ ∃s : P (D ∣ S = s) =  P (D) 1 2 P (D = tea ∣ S = I) = =  = P (D = tea) 2 3 ​ ​ Here the distribution changes with context, so subject and drink are dependent. Probability Foundations 34 / 101 Markov Assumption A language model could use the full history. A Markov assumption keeps only recent context.

No context Recent context Full history p(tea) p(tea | like) p(tea | I like) Ignore the history. Keep a short window. Keep everything before. p(xt ∣ x<t ) ≈ p(xt ∣ xt−k:t−1 ) ​ ​ ​ ​ A Markov model keeps dependence on recent context and drops older context. N-gram Models 37 / 101 Why Full History Is Hard to Estimate Ideally, use the entire history: p(xt ∣ x1 , … , xt−1 ) ​ ​ ​ Long histories rarely repeat → probabilities are hard to estimate reliably. N-gram Models 38 / 101 The Markov Idea: Use a Shorter History Longer history More information, but fewer repeated examples. Shorter history Less information, but easier probability estimation. The Markov assumption trades context length for estimability.

N-gram Models 39 / 101 Markov Assumption → N-gram p(xt ∣ x<t ) ≈ p^N (xt ∣ ht ), ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ht := xt−N +1:t−1 ​ ​ memory used to model context ht predict tea unigram, N = 1 ∅ nothing bigram, N = 2 xt−1 like trigram, N = 3 xt−2:t−1 I like An N-gram model remembers the previous N−1 tokens when predicting the next one. The assumption chooses the memory length; the N-gram model estimates probabilities inside that window. more contexts more evidence can truncate history → → match be counted together The real statistical benefit of the Markov assumption is evidence pooling. N-gram Models 46 / 101 Failure 1: An Unseen Context Query: p̂ 3(tea | I drink) Every token is familiar But the context is new Both I and drink occur in the corpus. C(I drink) = 0, so there is no row to normalize. The issue is not that “I drink” is impossible language; this particular context was simply never observed in training. Unseen context = no empirical evidence for any next-token distribution. N-gram Models 47 / 101 Failure 2: A Seen Context Can Still Predict Zero Query: p̂ 2(drink | I) Context was seen Pair was unseen C(I) = 2, so the denominator exists

and C(I, drink) = 0 ⇒ p̂ (drink | I) = 0. 2 the row is well-defined. drink is in the vocabulary, and “I drink” is perfectly plausible language. Zero only means “not observed in this training corpus.” Seen context + unseen continuation gives a valid distribution with an overconfident zero. N-gram Models 48 / 101 Sparsity Leads to Zero Counts longer context → fewer repeats → zero counts The problem Unseen events get zero probability. One simple fix: smoothing Reserve some probability mass for unseen events. Smoothing fixes zero probabilities — but not the underlying sparsity. Maximum Likelihood & Loss 53 / 101 Probability and Likelihood Ask Different Questions Probability Likelihood Fix θ; compare possible outcomes. Fix the observed x; compare parameters. pθ(x) L(θ; x) = pθ(x) What is likely under this model? Which parameters best support what we observed? Observed: I like → tea. If pθA(tea | I like) = 0.9 and pθB(tea | I like) = 0.2, the observation gives higher likelihood to θA. The numerical expression is the same; what we hold fixed and what we vary changes the question.

Maximum Likelihood & Loss 54 / 101 One Sentence Gives Many Likelihood Factors <s> I like tea <e> gives one observed next-token target at every position. <s> → I · I → like · I like → tea · … → <e> T +1 L(θ; x1:T ) = ∏ pθ (xt ∣ x<t ), ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ xT +1 = ⟨e⟩ ​ t=1 Each observed token contributes one conditional-probability factor; the final factor is the decision to stop. A sequence is likely when the model gives high probability to its observed next token at every position. Maximum Likelihood & Loss 55 / 101 The Dataset Likelihood Multiplies All Observed Decisions Training data contains many sequences, and every token position provides one observed prediction.

L(θ; D) = ∏ ∏ pθ (xt ∣ x<t ) (i) (i) ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ i t Data stay fixed θ changes The corpus tells us which next tokens Different parameters assign different actually occurred. probabilities to those observations. i indexes training sequences; t indexes positions inside each sequence. Dataset likelihood is one joint score for how well θ supports all observed training decisions. Maximum Likelihood & Loss 57 / 101 Maximum Likelihood Chooses the Best Parameters Which θ makes the observed training data most probable? θ^MLE = arg max L(θ; D) = arg max pθ (D) ​ ​ ​ ​ θ θ compare candidate choose highest observed data → → θ likelihood Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) chooses the parameters that give the observed data the greatest support. MLE turns “fit the training data” into a precise parameter-selection rule. Maximum Likelihood & Loss 58 / 101 N-gram Counting Was Already MLE After like, the corpus observed: tea, coffee, tea. One unknown probability Likelihood of what we saw Let q = p(tea | like).
